questions.text: An infant is delivered at 36 weeks of gestation. How is this infant best classified?

answers.text: Premature — born before 38 weeks and considered high risk
Mature — within the normal 38–42 week range
Post-term and at risk for meconium aspiration
Congenital, because prematurity is a birth defect

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the ductus arteriosus in the fetus?

answers.text: It connects the pulmonary artery and the aorta, shunting blood away from the non-functional lungs
It connects the liver and the inferior vena cava, returning blood quickly to the heart
It connects the two atria, shunting blood from the right to the left atrium
It connects the umbilical vein to the placenta for gas exchange

questions.text: After birth, what change in the pulmonary capillaries triggers constriction of the ductus arteriosus?

answers.text: A rise in PaO₂ (and a drop in prostaglandin) sensed by the vessel smooth muscle
A fall in PaO₂ with a rise in pulmonary vascular resistance
An increase in prostaglandin levels that closes the duct
A drop in systemic vascular resistance below pulmonary vascular resistance

questions.text: A neonate is found to have a ductal-dependent congenital heart defect. Which agent is given to maintain patency of the ductus arteriosus?

answers.text: Prostaglandin
Surfactant
Indomethacin
Beractant

questions.text: The foramen ovale normally closes about three weeks after birth. What change is primarily responsible for sealing it?

answers.text: An increase in left-sided heart pressure (SVR) that presses a flap of tissue over the opening
An increase in pulmonary vascular resistance above systemic vascular resistance
Clamping of the umbilical cord, which closes it directly
A rise in prostaglandin that constricts the interatrial septum

questions.text: A 38-year-old mother with gestational diabetes is in labor. Based on maternal risk factors, which adverse outcomes are most associated with her history?

answers.text: Large gestational age, congenital malformations, RDS, and hypoglycemia (diabetes); plus prematurity and chromosomal defects (age > 35)
Small for gestational age and facial dysmorphology from her diabetes
Low birth weight and prematurity, typical of mothers under 17 years
Sudden infant death syndrome, the hallmark outcome of gestational diabetes

questions.text: A pregnant patient presents with the placenta attached over the cervix. Which condition does this describe, and what is a key risk?

answers.text: Placenta previa — increased risk of prematurity, bleeding, and small gestational age
Abruptio placentae — fetal asphyxia from the placenta detaching from the uterine wall
Nuchal cord — compression of the cord around the infant's neck
Occult cord prolapse — compression of the cord within the uterus

questions.text: An amniocentesis returns an L/S ratio of 2:1 and phosphatidylglycerol greater than 1%. What do these results indicate?

answers.text: Mature lungs with stable surfactant production and a low chance of respiratory distress
Surfactant deficiency with a high likelihood of RDS at birth
The presence of meconium in the amniotic fluid
A chromosomal abnormality detected from sloughed fetal cells

questions.text: During labor, the fetal heart rate is noted to be 175 beats/min. How should this finding be interpreted?

answers.text: Tachycardia (normal is 100–160 beats/min), which can indicate fetal hypoxemia, prematurity, or maternal fever
A normal fetal heart rate that requires no further evaluation
Bradycardia indicating cord compression
A severe deceleration of more than 45 beats/min

questions.text: A neonate is delivered by cesarean section. Compared with a vaginal delivery, which difference is most clinically relevant for the respiratory therapist?

answers.text: The infant does not get "squeezed" through the birth canal, so lung secretions/fluid are not cleared as effectively
The infant retains more fetal hemoglobin, causing cyanosis
The ductus venosus fails to close because the cord is not clamped
The infant is always premature and requires surfactant
